rows.label: A pleasing aroma; a fragrant offering
rows.note: The text's own phrase: “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” in the laws of Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers, the first time at Gen 8:21 after Noah's burnt offerings, and taken up at Eph 5:2 and Phil 4:18 (“a fragrant offering”). rows.label: Isaac: “offer him as a burnt offering”, “the lamb for the burnt offering”
rows.note: Genesis 22 as the verses have it: the word to Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering”, and the ram offered “in place of his son”. Heb 11:17 and Jas 2:21 take it up, the second inside an argument about faith and works (see the faith page). Readers part on what the story shows -- a test of Abraham, a substitute provided, a picture of a later sacrifice -- and the page takes no side. The children given to other gods are the row further down.

rows.label: Eating from the sacrifice
rows.note: Where worshipers, priests or guests eat of a sacrifice (Gen 31:54; Lev 7:15; Deut 12:27), and where the New Testament speaks of eating food sacrificed to idols (1 Cor 8:10; Rev 2:14) and of “those who eat the sacrifices” as “fellow partakers in the altar” (1 Cor 10:18). What the shared meal means -- fellowship with the LORD, a gift received from Him, a sharing in what is offered -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side. The LORD's own “sacrificial feast” for the birds and beasts is here too (Ezek 39:17-19). The fire that consumes a sacrifice is not here; it is under “Every other use”.

rows.label: The Passover
rows.note: The text calls it a sacrifice (Exod 12:27; 34:25; Deut 16:2), names the day “when the Passover lamb was sacrificed” (Mark 14:12; Luke 22:7), and Paul writes “Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed” (1 Cor 5:7). How the Passover and the death of Christ are related, readers take differently; the page sets the verses side by side and takes no side.

rows.label: Blood beside sacrifice
rows.note: Blood is named in the same verse as the sacrifice: put on the altar (Lev 4:7), sprinkled (Ezek 43:18), not to be offered with leaven (Exod 23:18), and in the Council's letter forbidden to eat (Acts 15:29). The prophets also picture a day of judgment as the LORD's own sacrifice, “bathed in blood” (Isa 34:6; Jer 46:10; Ezek 39:17-19). What the blood does -- covers, cleanses, ransoms, gives a life for a life -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side. Lev 17:11 and Heb 9:22, which have no word for sacrifice, are among the verses at the head of the page.

rows.label: Atonement made; a hand laid on the head
rows.note: The text says the priest “will make atonement” for the offerer with the offering, and in Lev 4:26 and 5:10 “he will be forgiven”; it says the offerer “lays his hand on the head” of the offering (Lev 1:4; 4:24). What atonement does -- covers, cleanses, ransoms, turns away wrath -- and what the hand laid on the head does -- identifies, dedicates, transfers -- readers take differently, and the page takes no side. The Hebrew is כִּפֶּר, a different word from the one for forgive (see forgiveness, where the two are set side by side). The sin offering of Lev 4-5 is also under “Sacrifice and sin”, below.

rows.note: In Hebrew חַטָּאת is both 'sin' and 'sin offering'; the Berean prints 'sin offering' where the verse is about the offering, and the verse reads 'sins' where it is not (Isa 43:24; Hos 8:13). Heb 10:26 (“no further sacrifice for sins remains”) stands here with Heb 10:12 and 10:18; where Christian traditions part on whether a believer can fall away, and on what Heb 10:26 says of it, the page takes no side. The sin offering's ritual in Lev 4-5 is also in the row “Atonement made; a hand laid on the head”, above.

rows.label: Sacrifice set beside what the LORD asks: not desired, not accepted, “mercy, not sacrifice”
rows.note: Set side by side as the text has them: “obedience is better than sacrifice” (1 Sam 15:22), “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire” (Ps 40:6; Heb 10:5, 8), “I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6; Matt 9:13; 12:7), and the sacrifices He does not accept (Isa 1:11; Jer 6:20; 14:12; Amos 5:22; Hos 8:13). Readers part on whether these verses set the sacrifices of the law aside, or reject only a sacrifice offered without mercy, justice and obedience; and on how Ps 40:6 (“my ears You have opened”) stands to Heb 10:5 (“a body You prepared for Me”), which the Berean prints differently. In Jer 7:22 the Berean reads “did not merely command them”; the Hebrew has no word for “merely”. Amos 5:25 (“Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness?”), quoted at Acts 7:42, is a question and stands under “Every other use”; readers part on what answer it expects. The page takes no side.

Readers part on whether these replace the offerings of the law or stand beside them; the page takes no side.

rows.label: The Lord's table: “This is My body”, blood “poured out”, “in remembrance of Me”, “a participation”
rows.note: The words of the Last Supper and Paul on the table: “Take and eat; this is My body” (Matt 26:26; Mark 14:22), “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt 26:28; Mark 14:24 has “which is poured out for many”), “do this in remembrance of Me” (Luke 22:19; 1 Cor 11:24-25), “a participation in the blood of Christ” (1 Cor 10:16), “those who eat the sacrifices ... fellow partakers in the altar” (1 Cor 10:18), “the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Cor 10:21). Only 1 Cor 10:18 has a word for sacrifice; the others are here because they speak of the body, the blood, the covenant and the meal. The covenant sealed with burnt and peace offerings and “the blood of the covenant” is at Exod 24:5-8 (Exod 24:5 is under “Sacrificed to the LORD”, in the verb form). The other words of the tellings of the Supper (Matt 26:27; 1 Cor 11:23, 26) are not set here, having no word for sacrifice. Readers part on whether the Lord's Supper is itself a sacrifice, a memorial, a participation in Christ's body and blood, or more than one of these; the page takes no side.

rows.label: Hebrews: offered again and again, unable to cleanse; once for all
rows.note: Hebrews on the sacrifices of the law and the sacrifice of Christ: “the same sacrifices offered year after year” (10:1), “again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins” (10:11), “gifts and sacrifices being offered were unable to cleanse the conscience” (9:9); and “once for all ... by the sacrifice of Himself” (9:26), “the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (10:10), “one sacrifice for sins” (10:12), “a single offering” (10:14). Heb 9:26 names Christ, and 10:10 Jesus Christ; 7:27, 10:12 and 10:14 say “He” or “this Priest” inside the same argument. Readers part on whether the sacrifices of the law are fulfilled in Christ's, ended by it, or continue in some form, and on how “once for all” stands to the Lord's table; the page takes no side. The rows above say what the law's offerings were given for, for example the priest “will make atonement for that man's sin, and he will be forgiven” (Lev 4:26); the page says nothing on how that stands to Heb 9:9 or 10:1.

words.note: חַטָּאת is one Hebrew word for 'sin' and for the 'sin offering'; the Berean prints 'sin offering' where the verse is about the offering. It is a different word from זֶבַח.

eg.text: But burn the flesh of the bull and its hide and dung outside the camp; it is a sin offering.
If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people, he must bring to the LORD a young bull without blemish as a sin offering for the sin he has committed.

words.note: עָלָה is the verb 'go up'; the Berean prints 'offered up' where the thing that goes up is the burnt offering. The noun עֹלָה is one of the hub's own words.

eg.text: Then Noah built an altar to the LORD. And taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar.
Then Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. So he went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them: When any of you brings an offering to the LORD, you may bring as your offering an animal from the herd or the flock.
If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he is to present an unblemished male. He must bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD.
Then burn the entire ram on the altar; it is a burnt offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
Then take them from their hands and burn them on the altar atop the burnt offering as a pleasing aroma before the LORD; it is a food offering to the LORD.
So Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him-a stone marker-and he poured out a drink offering on it and anointed it with oil.
With the first lamb offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, mixed with a quarter hin of oil from pressed olives, and a drink offering of a quarter hin of wine.

words.note: שֶׁלֶם (plural שְׁלָמִים) is the 'peace offering', a kind of זֶבַח in Lev 3 and 7; it is a different word.

eg.text: You are to make for Me an altar of earth, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and goats and cattle. In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you.
Along with his peace offering of thanksgiving he is to present an offering with cakes of leavened bread.
If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he is to present an unblemished male. He must bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD.
The entrails and legs must be washed with water, and the priest shall present all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

words.note: אָשָׁם is the 'guilt offering' (and 'guilt'); a different word from זֶבַח.

eg.text: “If someone acts unfaithfully and sins unintentionally against any of the LORD's holy things, he must bring his guilt offering to the LORD: an unblemished ram from the flock, of proper value in silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel; it is a guilt offering.
